# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Review: Two-year follow-up (Varden trial and Halden subset)

This report answers questions the earlier papers left open, and it does so well. It adds a log-based hours measure, registers the mediation analysis before the outcomes were available, and checks the meta-analysis's four long-follow-up studies directly.

**What checks out:**
- **Output per hour:** 0.966 / 0.88 = +9.8% on timesheets, and 0.966 / 0.89 = +8.5% on logs.
- **Halden continuers:** 96.8 / 0.866 = +11.8%, with 34.9 / 40.3 = −13.4% hours.
- **Mediation shares** sum to 100%.

**Where the conclusions hold:**
- **Against "entirely an artifact":** Varden now meets every standard Varga & Holm proposed, and a gain remains.
- **Against "no sign of decay":** if the four long studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, they cannot speak to decay. That is the confound I suspected.

The issues below mainly affect how much decline the data show and what the mediation result means.

## Main issues

**1. Control offices changed their meetings partway through, which affects the 24-month estimate.**
- In month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their recurring meetings and saw output per hour rise by about 4%.
- That improves the comparison group for months 15–24, which pushes the difference-in-differences estimate toward zero.
- So some of the apparent decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may be the control group improving, not the treatment effect fading.
- The audit may also have been prompted by the trial itself, since control staff knew it was running and the meetings finding was public by then.
- The authors present this only as an "unplanned observation." It should be handled as a threat to the main estimate:
  - Report the 24-month estimates with these two offices excluded.
  - Alternatively, report estimates for months 10–15 separately.
- A side note on the averages: if those two offices fell by about 2.1 hours each and the control mean moved only from 7.2 to 7.0, the other five control offices must have *increased* meeting time by about half an hour each. That is plausible, but worth confirming.

**2. The size of the decline is overstated and not statistically established.**
- The Summary compares 12.5% at nine months (timesheets) with 8.5% at 24 months (logs). These are different measures.
- The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% → 9.8%, as the body says. That is a fall of about a fifth (2.7 / 12.5), not "about a quarter" as §5 states.
- More importantly, the two confidence intervals (6.9–18.4 and 4.6–15.2) overlap heavily. The decline could be noise, or partly the control-office issue above.
- "Consistent with some fading" is fair. Using the decline as an established finding against the meta-analysis is not. The defensible claim is that durability beyond nine months is now *possible to assess*, and the gain clearly persists. Whether it has shrunk is uncertain.

**3. The mediation result is weaker than "confirms."**
- **It is not an independent test.** The hypothesis came from these same seven treated offices, and the 24-month data overlap with the months that generated it. A registered analysis prevents analytic flexibility, but it is not a replication.
- **The effective sample is 14 offices, not the office-months.** Counting office-months as a "larger sample" overstates the information unless clustering is fully accounted for. With 7 v 7 clusters, the 28–66% CI looks narrow. The inference method should be stated, and preferably checked with randomisation inference or a wild-cluster bootstrap.
- **Mediators are not randomised.** Any office-level factor that affects both meeting cuts and output would bias the shares. Managerial quality is the obvious example. The Limitations note this, but "confirms" in the Summary should become something like "supports."

**4. It is unclear what log-in time measures, and this affects the mediation result.**
- Log-in time is "active log-in time on the case-management system." That probably *excludes* meetings, so it is a different construct from timesheet hours, not simply a stricter version of them.
- **If logs exclude meetings:** cutting meetings would move time *into* logged case work. Log hours should then have fallen much less than timesheet hours, roughly 5% rather than 11% on the reported figures. They didn't.
- **If logs include meeting time:** a rough calculation from the reported figures suggests that removing about 3.3 hours of meetings could, on its own, account for nearly all of the gain, assuming meetings produce no case output. That would make 47% look *low*.
  - Treated non-meeting hours: ≈ 0.89 × 37.9 − 3.9 ≈ 29.8
  - Control non-meeting hours: ≈ 37.9 − 7.0 ≈ 30.9
  - Output ratio is 0.966, so output per non-meeting hour is roughly unchanged.
- Either way, the paper needs to say what logs capture and how meeting time sits in the denominator. The interpretation of the mediation shares depends on it.

**5. Baseline meeting data are new.**
- The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six.
- This report gives baselines (7.4 and 7.2). It should explain where those came from, presumably calendars retrieved retrospectively.
- It should also say whether the data are complete and comparable across offices, because the mediation analysis depends on them.

## The counter-office figures

- **Staffing.** Restoring the number of *contacts handled* needs about 1 / 0.886 ≈ 13% more staff, which matches the county's 12%. But restoring *waiting times* is a different target.
  - Much of the counter per-hour gain was probably higher utilisation: less idle time between customers.
  - That gain disappears once staff are added.
  - Restoring staffed hours would need closer to 1 / 0.83 ≈ 20% more staff.
- **Cost.** 12% more staff at unchanged pay, handling roughly baseline volume, implies about +12–13% cost per contact, not 9%. The county's figure may rest on assumptions not stated here, and these should be given.

## Halden subset

- **Further selection.** Only 14 of the 23 organisations with records agreed to take part. The report correctly calls the 11 continuers "survivors twice over."
- **"Upper bound" is too strong.** There is no comparison group, background trends could go either way, and time tracking may undercount. "Likely optimistic" is accurate; "upper bound" is not guaranteed.
- **The baseline hours look borrowed.** 40.3 is exactly the 27-organisation figure from Varga & Holm. Is it the baseline for these 11 organisations specifically?
- **The reversions are informative.**
  - The marketing agency reverted, citing client deadlines. That is not a coverage obligation in the meta-analysis's sense.
  - The Summary's "all with client-facing or coverage obligations" stretches to include it.
  - It suggests that discretionary work with external deadlines may behave partly like coverage-bound work. It is worth saying so rather than folding it into the existing categories.

## Points carried over from the nine-month report

Several items are still unaddressed:
- Few-cluster inference for the main estimates.
- Sick days per *scheduled day*: the −27% may still be partly mechanical.
- Overtime cost in case-processing.
- Backlog size or age, to show output is sustainable.
- Appeal and resignation figures as difference-in-differences estimates with CIs, rather than raw treated-versus-control comparisons.

## Independence

The Halden lead author co-authors this report, which assesses criticism of the Halden pilot. That is not a problem in itself, and the Halden section is suitably cautious. Still, it is worth stating, and the decisive evidence remains the Varden trial.

## Where things stand now

| Question | Status after this report |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain in discretionary (case) work | Persists at 24 months in the best-designed study: about 8.5–10%, with per-worker output about 3% below control (CI includes zero). |
| Decay | The gain hasn't vanished. Whether it has shrunk is unclear, given overlapping CIs and control-office contamination. |
| Coverage-bound work | Settled for practical purposes: the county ended that arm because of service levels. |
| Mechanism | Meeting reduction is the leading candidate, but not independently confirmed. The log-hours definition needs resolving before the 47% can be interpreted. |
| Hours cut versus reorganisation | Open. No arm reorganised without cutting hours. An arm doing a meeting audit with no hours change is the obvious next trial. |
